name: Saint Barthélemy
summary_text: Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.  No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.  Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered on an island of about 8 square miles with roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.  Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. Detainees held in Saint Barthélemy fall under that same system. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.  An aggregate index rates the collectivity 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.  Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors.

sources.title: Law of 18 November 2016 on modernisation of justice - transgender legal gender change, effective 1 Jan 2017
sources.documents: Allows transgender people to legally change gender without surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates; requires court order; first-name change at registry office - core gender-recognition machinery for trans visitors/residents.
sources.detail: No URL visible; citation detail: Senate approved 6 Nov 2015, National Assembly 24 May 2016 and modified version 12 July 2016, Senate discussed 28 Sept, National Assembly plenary 12 Oct rejected medical-treatment amendments, Constitutional Council ruled constitutional 17 Nov, signed 18 Nov 2016, published Journal Officiel next day, took effect 1 Jan 2017; introduced by MP Pascale Crozon

sources.title: Law of 31 December 2004 amending anti-discrimination legislation and Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881
sources.documents: Criminalizes homophobic/sexist/racist comments, injury/defamation/insult/incitement; increases penalties for assault/murder motivated by sexual orientation; created Haute autorite de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'egalite - hate-crime enforcement machinery.
sources.detail: No URL visible; citation detail: National Assembly approved 31 Dec 2004, max penalty 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment; Title 3 and articles 20 and 21 amended Press Law of 29 July 1881; first conviction Jan 2006 of MP Christian Vanneste later cancelled by Court of Cassation; 2017 transphobia became aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison

sources.title: B. v France - European Court of Human Rights (1992)
sources.documents: Court ruling that required France to allow legal gender change after decades-long legislative ban, even with medical/surgical transition; foundational trans-rights precedent.
sources.detail: No URL visible; citation detail: cited as 1992 case B. vs France at the European Court of Human Rights changed ban; context includes 1959 Coccinelle legal change with lawyer Robert Badinter and 1962 marriage recognition before ban

sources.documents: Institutional/human-rights monitoring: lack of self-determination, waiting times, inequitable access, recommendation for informed consent; DILCRAH Interministerial Delegation for Fight Against Racism, Anti-Semitism and Anti-LGBT Hatred as rights machinery; plus 2014 study and parliamentary vote data contextualizing Saint Barthelemy - same-sex marriage legal in all overseas, deputy for Saint Martin and Saint Barthelemy voted against, but Saint Barthelemy described as more open/relaxed due to international celebrity tourism vs other French Caribbean.
sources.detail: No URL visible; citation detail: ILGA-Europe report published 2022; DILCRAH scientific committee controversy 2022 involving Little Mermaid Observatory; overseas deputies vote: 11 for, 11 against including 1 from Saint Martin and Saint Barthelemy, 1 abstained, 3 absent; 2014 study: about 20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as sexuality like any other vs 77% metropolitan France

name: Bermuda
summary_text: Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory. Local legislation governs, and the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; United Kingdom measures could be applied only by Order in Council.  The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, striking two sections of the Criminal Code. The debate divided the island, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change.  In July 2013 the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and, in the same instrument, on grounds of age. Same-sex marriage was not permitted at that point.  The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act in February 2018. It replaced same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships open to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. Recognition of a same-sex partner therefore rests on the partnership register rather than on marriage.
